unit.title: Perform basic welding using oxyacetylene welding process (OAW) - fuel gas welding

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which eye protection is right for oxy-acetylene welding of thin mild steel?
options: Clear safety glasses with no tint
Goggles or a visor of about shade 4 to 6
An arc welding helmet with a shade 13 filter
Ordinary dark sunglasses

questions.stem: Why must gas welding be done well away from oil, paint tins and rags?
options: Their smell makes the flame burn yellow
They make the filler rods rust much faster
They stop the flux from melting
Sparks and hot metal can set them on fire

questions.stem: Which clothing is safe for oxy-acetylene welding?
options: Cotton overalls, leather gloves and boots
Nylon overalls and rubber gloves
Shorts, a T-shirt and canvas shoes
A polyester shirt with the sleeves rolled up

questions.stem: Why must an acetylene cylinder always stand upright?
options: So the gauge can be read more easily
So the cylinder takes up less floor space
So the acetone inside stays in the cylinder
So the valve on top stays cooler in the hot sun

questions.stem: Inside an acetylene cylinder, the gas is…
options: Pumped in as a liquid, like LPG cooking gas
Dissolved in acetone held in a porous filling
Already mixed with oxygen, ready for welding
Stored at the same high pressure as oxygen

questions.stem: Why must copper pipe, or fittings with a lot of copper in them, never be used for acetylene?
options: Acetylene forms an explosive compound with copper
Copper pipe is too soft to hold the gas pressure
Copper makes the flame burn green and cooler
Copper pipe blocks up with soot from the gas

questions.stem: How should gas cylinders be moved around the workshop?
options: Rolled along the floor on their sides
Dragged along by the valve or regulator
On a trolley, chained, with valves shut
Carried on the shoulder by one person

questions.stem: How are fuel gas fittings made different from oxygen fittings?
options: Fuel gas fittings are made of plastic
Fuel gas fittings have no threads at all
Fuel gas fittings are much larger in size
Fuel gas fittings have left-hand threads

questions.stem: What does a regulator do?
options: Mixes the two gases before the torch
Lowers the gas to a steady working pressure
Lights the torch as soon as the valve is opened
Measures the heat of the flame at the tip

questions.stem: Where are flashback arrestors normally fitted on an oxy-acetylene set?
options: At both regulators, and often at the torch
On the oxygen hose only, near the torch
Inside the nozzle tip, behind the hole
On the cylinder trolley, under the cylinders

questions.stem: When opening a cylinder valve, where should you stand?
options: Directly in front of the regulator gauges
Right behind the cylinder with your face over it
To the side of the regulator, not in front
As far away as the hose will reach

questions.stem: How far should a key-operated acetylene cylinder valve normally be opened?
options: All the way open, then turned back half a turn
Just a crack, so the gauge barely moves
Fully open, so the gas flows freely
About 1½ turns at most, key left on

questions.stem: Why are the hoses purged before the torch is lit?
options: To warm the hoses up in the morning
To clear out any mixed gas or air from the hoses
To check that both gauges are reading the right way
To cool the regulators before lighting up

questions.stem: When lighting an oxy-acetylene torch, what is done first?
options: Open the fuel gas valve a little and light it
Open the oxygen valve fully, then light it
Open both valves fully and light with a match
Light the oxygen alone, then add the acetylene

questions.stem: How does a neutral flame look?
options: A long, white feather around the inner cone
A short, sharp, pointed cone that hisses loudly
A clear, rounded inner cone with no feather
A yellow, smoky flame with black soot

questions.stem: Which flame has extra acetylene and shows a white feather beyond the inner cone?
options: A neutral flame
An oxidising flame
A cutting flame
A carburising flame

questions.stem: Which flame is used for welding mild steel?
options: An oxidising flame
A neutral flame
A carburising flame
A pure acetylene flame

questions.stem: What happens when mild steel is welded with an oxidising flame?
options: The pool sparks and the weld turns brittle
The weld becomes softer and stronger than normal
The flame goes out every few seconds
The filler rod will not melt at all

questions.stem: Where is the hottest part of an oxy-acetylene flame?
options: At the far end of the outer flame
Inside the nozzle, before the gas comes out
Just beyond the tip of the inner cone
In the yellow smoke at the edge

questions.stem: How is the right nozzle (tip) size chosen?
options: Always the biggest nozzle, as it suits any job
By metal thickness, from the maker's chart
By the colour of the coating on the filler rod
By how full the cylinders are

questions.stem: How are the working pressures for oxygen and acetylene set?
options: Both as high as the regulators will allow
Oxygen at full cylinder pressure, acetylene low
By listening to the sound of the gas at the torch
From the maker's chart for the nozzle size used

questions.stem: Which filler rod is normally used for gas welding mild steel?
options: Copper-coated steel rod
Bare brass brazing rod
Pure aluminium rod
Flux-coated stainless rod

questions.stem: Why is no flux needed when gas welding mild steel with a neutral flame?
options: Mild steel melts too fast for flux to work
The filler rod already has a thick flux coating
The outer flame shields the pool from the air
Flux would put the flame out

questions.stem: In the leftward (forehand) method, where is the filler rod held?
options: Behind the flame, over the finished weld
In front of the flame, ahead of the pool
Under the plate, on the back of the joint
Inside the flame's inner cone all the time

questions.stem: Leftward welding is mainly used on which work?
options: Thick plate over about 12 mm
Cast iron engine blocks
Large, heavy structural beams
Thin steel, up to about 5 mm

questions.stem: How far should the tip of the inner cone be from the weld pool?
options: About 2–3 mm, close but not touching
Pushed down right into the pool itself
About 50 mm away, well clear of it
As far as the flame will reach

questions.stem: What can happen if the nozzle tip touches the weld pool?
options: The flame gets hotter and welds faster
The gas pressure in the cylinder rises
The nozzle can block and cause a backfire
The rod melts down into a neat, round bead

questions.stem: What is a backfire?
options: A flame that burns back up the hose to the cylinder
A pop as the flame snaps back into the nozzle
A leak at the regulator that hisses
Soot that blows out of the nozzle

questions.stem: What should you do if a flashback happens (a squeal or hiss, and the flame burning inside the torch or hose)?
options: Keep welding and wait for it to stop by itself
Pour water on the hose to cool it down
Turn up the oxygen to blow the flame out
Shut the torch and cylinder valves at once

questions.stem: Why are tacks placed along a thin-sheet butt joint before it is welded?
options: To stop the gap closing as the sheet heats
To give the welder a place to rest the rod
To mark where each new rod should begin
To make the sheet heavier so it does not move

questions.stem: For very thin sheet (under about 1.5 mm), which edge preparation helps stop burn-through?
options: A wide single-V with a big root gap
A double-V bevel on both sides
Flanged (turned-up) edges that melt down
A square edge with a 5 mm gap left open

questions.stem: Why is the torch moved with a slight side-to-side motion in leftward welding?
options: To keep the gas cool in the hose
To melt both edges evenly into the pool
To blow slag off the top of the pool
To stop the cylinder valves from freezing

questions.stem: What is the right way to add filler rod in gas welding?
options: Melt it in the flame and let it drip onto the plate
Hold it in the inner cone until it glows red
Push it hard against the cold plate ahead
Dip it into the front edge of the pool

questions.stem: Which joint is formed when two sheets meet at their edges to make an L shape?
options: A lap joint
A butt joint
A corner joint
A plug joint

questions.stem: What causes burn-through (holes) in thin-sheet gas welds?
options: A nozzle too big, or moving too slowly
Too little heat, from a nozzle that is too small
Using a copper-coated filler rod on steel
Holding the rod ahead of the flame

questions.stem: What does lack of fusion in a gas weld mean?
options: The weld has spattered over the plate
The filler has not melted into the edges
The weld is too wide and too flat
The weld has a crack along the top

questions.stem: Why should the crater at the end of a gas weld be filled?
options: To use up every last bit of the filler rod
To make the end of the weld look shiny
To let the flame burn off all the gas left in the hose
Craters can crack and weaken the end of the weld

questions.stem: Which is a sign of a good butt weld on thin sheet?
options: Holes along the joint where the sheet melted away
A wide groove left along each side of the weld
Even ripples, with even penetration underneath
Filler sitting on top with the edges still visible

questions.stem: At the end of the day, both torch valves and both cylinder valves are closed. What is done next?
options: Leave the gas in the hoses for tomorrow
Take off the regulators with gas still in them
Turn the regulator screws in fully to hold pressure
Bleed the hoses, then close the torch valves

questions.stem: Why must oxygen never be used to blow dust off your clothes?
options: Oxygen-soaked clothes can catch fire fast
Oxygen leaves a white stain on the clothes
Oxygen is too cold and can freeze the skin
Oxygen makes the cylinder empty too fast

questions.stem: Which gives a safe leak test on an oxy-acetylene set?
options: A small flame passed along each joint
Soapy water brushed on each joint
Your nose held close to each fitting
Grease rubbed on to seal every joint

questions.stem: What should you do with a hot welded test piece?
options: Hand it straight to the next person
Leave it on the floor where people walk
Pick it up by hand once it stops glowing
Hold it with tongs and mark it HOT

questions.stem: Shanice gets a spark of hot metal in her eye. What should be done first?
options: Rub the eye hard to get the spark out
Put a few drops of oil into the eye
Rinse with eyewash and get first aid
Carry on and see if it feels better tomorrow

questions.stem: Before starting a gas welding job, what should you check on the job sheet?
options: The metal, its thickness and the joint to be made
The colour of paint to put on the finished job
The name of the gas supplier
The date on which the cylinders were last filled

questions.stem: A regulator gauge glass is cracked and the needle sticks. What should you do?
options: Tap the gauge until the needle moves again
Stop using it, label it faulty and report it
Guess the pressure from the sound of the gas
Swap the oxygen and acetylene regulators

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters OAW stand for?
What colour is the acetylene (fuel gas) hose?
What is the name of the small, bright, sharp part in the middle of the flame, at the nozzle?
What tool is used to light the torch?
What is the method called where the rod follows behind the flame and the weld moves from left to right (for a right-handed welder)?
What is the pool of melted metal under the flame called?
What is the gauge on a regulator called that shows the pressure going out to the hose?
What tool is used to clean a blocked nozzle hole?
What is the name for small holes in a weld caused by trapped gas?
What name is given to the metal being welded, as opposed to the filler rod?
What is the name of the joint where two sheets meet edge to edge in the same flat line?
Apart from the flashback arrestor, what valve at the torch stops gas flowing backwards into the hose?
What do the letters PPE stand for?
What document from the gas supplier gives the hazards of the gas and how to handle it?
After the hoses are bled, which part of each regulator is turned out so that no pressure is held on it?

essays.stem: Describe the main dangers of oxy-acetylene welding and how a welder controls each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Fire and explosion: acetylene burns very easily, and oxygen makes anything burn fiercely. Keep oil and grease off oxygen fittings, test for leaks with soapy water, fit flashback arrestors, keep cylinders upright and chained, and clear anything that burns from the area, with an extinguisher at hand. Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothes. Burns: the flame, the hot metal and sparks can burn the skin, so wear leather gloves, cotton overalls and boots, and handle hot work with tongs. Eye damage: the bright glow of the pool and flame can harm the eyes, so wear goggles of about shade 4 to 6. Fumes: welding dirty or coated metal gives off fumes, so work with good ventilation and keep your head out of the fumes. Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Fire and explosion: no oil on oxygen fittings, leak test with soapy water, arrestors, burnables cleared, extinguisher
Cylinders upright and chained; oxygen never used to blow off clothes
Burns: leather gloves, cotton clothing, boots, tongs for hot work
Eyes: tinted goggles of about shade 4 to 6
Fumes: ventilation, head kept out of the fumes

essays.stem: Explain how oxygen and acetylene cylinders must be stored, moved and secured in the workshop, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Cylinders must be kept upright and chained or strapped to a wall or trolley so that they cannot fall; a falling cylinder can break its valve and release the gas violently. Acetylene must always be upright so that the acetone inside does not come out with the gas. Store cylinders in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place, out of direct sun and away from heat, sparks and anything that burns. Keep oxygen apart from fuel gas cylinders, by a safe distance or a fire-resistant wall as the Centre's rules say, so that a fire at one is not fed by the other. Keep full and empty cylinders apart and labelled. Move cylinders on a proper trolley with the valves closed and caps fitted, never by rolling them or lifting them by the valve. Never let oil or grease touch an oxygen cylinder or valve.
markingPoints: Upright and chained or strapped so they cannot fall, and why
Acetylene upright so the acetone stays in the cylinder
Stored cool, dry and ventilated, away from heat, sun and burnables
Oxygen kept apart from fuel gas; full and empty cylinders kept apart
Moved on a trolley with valves closed; no oil or grease on oxygen

essays.stem: Describe how to assemble an oxy-acetylene welding set from the cylinders to the torch, and how to check it for leaks.
essays.modelAnswer: Check that both cylinders are chained upright on the trolley, and that the valve outlets are clean and free of oil and damage. Fit the oxygen regulator to the oxygen cylinder (right-hand thread) and the acetylene regulator to the acetylene cylinder (left-hand thread), and tighten them with the right spanner without forcing. Fit a flashback arrestor to each regulator outlet. Check the hoses for cracks, cuts and burns, then fit them: the red hose to the fuel gas and the other to oxygen. Fit non-return valves at the torch, then the torch, and choose a nozzle from the maker's chart. Make sure the regulator screws are released, stand to one side and open the cylinder valves slowly. Set the working pressures. Brush soapy water on every joint and look for bubbles; fix any leak with the gas off. Purge each hose before lighting.
markingPoints: Cylinders secured; valve outlets checked clean and free of oil
Each regulator fitted to the right gas (fuel left-hand, oxygen right-hand)
Flashback arrestors, checked hoses and non-return valves fitted the right way
Regulator screws released, valves opened slowly from the side, pressures set from the chart
Every joint leak tested with soapy water and hoses purged

essays.stem: Describe step by step how to light the torch and adjust it to a neutral flame, and then how to put the flame out safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Check that the right nozzle is fitted and that the working pressures are set from the maker's chart. Purge each hose for a few seconds. Point the torch away from people, the cylinders, the hoses and anything that can burn. Open the acetylene torch valve a little and light it at once with a spark lighter. Open the acetylene a little more until the flame stops giving off black smoke. Then slowly open the oxygen valve. The flame shows a white feather around the inner cone; keep adding oxygen until the feather just disappears into a clear, rounded inner cone. This is a neutral flame. Check it again from time to time while you work. To put the flame out, close the torch valves in the order the torch maker and the Centre's rules give, and hang the torch up safely.
markingPoints: Nozzle and pressures checked; hoses purged
Torch pointed away from people, cylinders, hoses and burnables
Fuel gas lit first with a spark lighter, and opened until the smoke stops
Oxygen added until the white feather just disappears (neutral flame)
Flame put out by closing the torch valves in the maker's order

essays.stem: Describe the three oxy-acetylene flames, how each one looks, and what each one is used for.
essays.modelAnswer: A neutral flame has about equal amounts of oxygen and acetylene. It has a clear, rounded inner cone with no feather and burns quietly. It adds nothing to the metal, so it is used for welding mild steel and for most general work. A carburising (reducing) flame has extra acetylene. It shows a white feather around the inner cone; the longer the feather, the more extra acetylene. It adds carbon to steel, so it is used only for special jobs such as hard-facing, not for normal steel welding. An oxidising flame has extra oxygen. Its inner cone is short, sharp and pointed, and it hisses loudly. It burns steel and makes the weld brittle and porous, so it is not used on steel, but a slightly oxidising flame is used with brass or bronze rod.
markingPoints: Neutral: equal gases, clear rounded cone, no feather, used for mild steel
Carburising: extra acetylene, white feather around the cone
Carburising adds carbon, used only for special jobs such as hard-facing
Oxidising: extra oxygen, short pointed cone, loud hiss
Oxidising makes steel welds brittle; slightly oxidising used for brass or bronze

essays.stem: Explain how to make a butt weld in 1.6 mm mild steel sheet using the leftward method.
essays.modelAnswer: Clean the edges of the sheets and lay them on firebricks with a small, even gap, or with the edges touching, as the instructor directs. Choose the nozzle from the chart for 1.6 mm and set a neutral flame. Tack the sheets at each end and then about every 50 mm, so that the gap does not close up as it heats. A right-handed welder starts at the right-hand end and works to the left. Hold the torch at about 60–70° to the sheet, pointing in the direction of travel, and the copper-coated rod at about 30–40° in front of the flame. Keep the tip of the inner cone about 2–3 mm above the pool. When both edges melt into a pool, dip the rod into the front of the pool and move steadily along with a slight side-to-side motion. Fill the crater at the end, then check the ripples and the penetration underneath.
markingPoints: Edges cleaned, gap set and sheets tacked at regular spacing
Nozzle chosen from the chart and a neutral flame set
Right to left, flame pointing ahead, with suitable torch and rod angles
Cone tip 2–3 mm off the pool; both edges melted before the rod is dipped in
Crater filled; ripples and penetration checked

essays.stem: Explain the difference between a backfire and a flashback. Give possible causes of each, and say what the welder must do.
essays.modelAnswer: A backfire is a loud pop when the flame snaps back into the nozzle. The flame may go out or light again by itself. It can be caused by touching the nozzle on the work or the pool, a nozzle that is overheated or blocked with spatter, or pressures set too low. Shut the torch valves, let the nozzle cool, clean it, check the pressures and relight. A flashback is much more dangerous: the flame burns back inside the torch and may travel up the hose towards the regulator. There is a squeal or hiss and the torch may get hot. It can be caused by wrong pressures, hoses that were not purged, or a leak. Close the torch valves at once (oxygen first), then the cylinder valves, and call the instructor. The torch, hoses and arrestors must be checked before the set is used again.
markingPoints: Backfire: a pop as the flame snaps back into the nozzle
Backfire causes (nozzle touching, hot or blocked nozzle, low pressure) and what to do
Flashback: flame burning back inside the torch or hose, with a squeal or hiss
Flashback action: torch valves shut at once, then cylinder valves
Instructor told and equipment checked before it is used again

essays.stem: Describe four faults that can be found in gas welds on thin sheet. For each, give a cause and a way to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Burn-through is holes melted right through the sheet. It is caused by too big a nozzle, too much heat or moving too slowly. Prevent it with the right nozzle and a steady speed. Lack of fusion is filler lying on the edges without melting into them. It is caused by too small a nozzle, moving too fast, or melting the rod before the edges have melted. Prevent it by forming a pool on both edges before adding rod. An oxidised, porous weld, with a lot of sparks from the pool, is caused by an oxidising flame. Prevent it by setting a neutral flame and checking it often. Distortion, where the sheet buckles, is caused by too much heat and too few tacks. Prevent it with tacks at regular spacing, the right nozzle and a steady speed.
markingPoints: Burn-through, with a correct cause and prevention
Lack of fusion, with a correct cause and prevention
Oxidised or porous weld from an oxidising flame, with prevention
Distortion (or another correct fault), with a cause and prevention
Uses correct trade terms throughout

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect a finished gas weld on thin sheet, and a simple test that could show whether it is sound.
essays.modelAnswer: First let the weld cool and clean it with a wire brush. Look at the top: the ripples should be even, the width and height steady, with no holes, cracks or burnt, sparkly surface, and the weld should blend into the sheet at both edges. Look at the back: there should be an even line of penetration all along the joint, with no burn-through and no places where the edges did not melt. Check that the sheets are still flat and in line, and that the crater at the end is filled. A simple test is a bend test. Cut a strip across the weld, clamp it in a vice with the weld just above the jaws, and bend it over with a hammer so that the back of the weld is stretched. A sound weld bends without cracking or opening up.
markingPoints: Cleans the weld and checks the face: even ripples and width, no holes or cracks
Checks the back for even penetration and no burn-through
Checks flatness, alignment and the end crater
Describes a bend test on a strip cut across the weld
States that a sound weld bends without cracking

essays.stem: Describe how to shut down an oxy-acetylene set at the end of the day, how to look after the hoses and nozzles, and what you would report.
essays.modelAnswer: Put out the flame by closing the torch valves in the maker's order. Close both cylinder valves. Open each torch valve in turn to bleed the gas from the hoses until both gauges read zero, then close the torch valves. Wind out the regulator adjusting screws so that no pressure is held on them. Coil the hoses loosely without kinks, and hang them up away from heat, oil and sharp edges. Let the nozzle cool, clean the hole with the right size of tip cleaner, and keep spare nozzles in their box. Wipe the torch clean, but never oil it. Leave the cylinders chained upright on the trolley. Report any leak, damaged hose, faulty gauge, repeated backfire or flashback to the instructor, and tag faulty parts out of use.
markingPoints: Flame put out in the maker's order, then cylinder valves closed
Hoses bled to zero and regulator screws released
Hoses coiled and stored away from heat, oil and sharp edges
Nozzle cooled and cleaned with a tip cleaner; no oil on the torch
Faults reported to the instructor and tagged out of use

practical1.title: Setting up an oxy-acetylene set, adjusting the flames and making fusion runs on thin sheet
practical1.brief: As a group, assemble an oxy-acetylene set on its trolley, leak test it and set the working pressures for a nozzle chosen from the maker's chart. Each member lights the torch, sets a carburising, a neutral and an oxidising flame for the photos, then makes the flame neutral again and puts it out, while the assessor watches. Then each member makes three straight fusion runs on 1.6 mm mild steel sheet by the leftward method: one without filler and two with copper-coated filler rod. Members check each other's runs for even width and penetration. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the work is finished and the area is clean.
materials: Oxy-acetylene set on a trolley, with regulators, flashback arrestors, hoses, torch and nozzles
Spark lighter, tip cleaners, and leak-test solution or soapy water
1.6 mm mild steel sheet, about 150 mm × 100 mm (one per member)
1.6 mm copper-coated mild steel filler rod
Firebricks, tongs, a wire brush and soapstone
photos: The set assembled on its trolley, with the cylinders chained
Soapy water on the joints during the leak test
A carburising flame, a neutral flame and an oxidising flame
A sheet with three fusion runs, top side
The back of the same sheet, showing the penetration
The set shut down, hoses coiled and the area clean
checklist: Wore gas welding goggles of a suitable shade, gloves, cotton overalls and boots
Helped to assemble the set with the right fittings and leak tested every joint
Purged the hoses and lit the torch safely with a spark lighter, fuel gas first
Set a neutral flame, and could show and name the other two flames
Made fusion runs of even width with the cone held just off the pool
Added filler by dipping it into the front of the pool
Shut down the set in the right order and bled the hoses
safety: Keep oil and grease away from all oxygen fittings
Test for leaks with soapy water, never with a flame
Point the torch away from people, cylinders and hoses when lighting it
Clear away anything that burns and keep an extinguisher at hand
Use tongs for hot sheet and mark it hot

practical2.title: Butt and outside corner joints in thin sheet by the leftward method, with a bend test
practical2.brief: As a group, weld butt joints and outside corner joints in 1.6 mm mild steel sheet (pieces about 150 mm × 50 mm) by the leftward method, using a neutral flame and copper-coated filler rod. Each member cleans, tacks and welds one butt joint and one corner joint while the assessor watches. Then the group cuts a strip across each member's butt joint and bends it in the vice to test it, and each member tells the assessor what the bend shows. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the work is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 1.6 mm mild steel sheet, about 150 mm × 50 mm (4 pieces per member)
1.6 mm copper-coated mild steel filler rod
Oxy-acetylene set with flashback arrestors, a nozzle chart and a spark lighter
Firebricks, tongs, pliers and a wire brush
Bench vice, hammer, and a hacksaw or snips for the bend test
photos: Sheets cleaned and tacked as a butt joint on firebricks
Sheets tacked as an outside corner joint
A finished butt weld, top side and back
The work area cleaned and the set shut down
checklist: Wore suitable PPE throughout, including tinted goggles and gloves
Cleaned the edges and tacked the joints at even spacing with the right gap
Chose the nozzle from the chart and set a neutral flame
Used the leftward method with suitable torch and rod angles
Welds show even ripples and full, even penetration, with no burn-through
Own bend-test strip bent without cracking, or the member explained why it cracked
Shut down the set safely and left the area tidy
safety: Keep cylinders upright and chained; keep oil off oxygen fittings
Work on firebricks, with burnables cleared and an extinguisher at hand
Use tongs and pliers for hot sheet; mark hot work
Wear gloves when handling cut sheet: the edges are sharp
Stand clear of the vice when bending: strips can spring
